The only thing this one doesn't talk much about is Columbus, I suppose because the author assumes he's been written about enough elsewhere. Honestly, I knew little about any of this, because the education system is garbage and I've been playing catch-up on history for a few years now.

Got a huge pile of books a few years back at a community book sale, for a few bucks apiece. I loaded up on history books. The meme is that you read history to avoid the mistakes of the past, and while that is one side effect, it's not the aim for me. Avoiding mistakes is like a chore, and not stimulating in itself. The main reason to read history is for context of the present. You begin to see the big picture of why things are the way they are, which is impossible to do by just looking at the present. It opens your mind to a whole new dimension. You can observe the present, but without history you cannot intimately understand it. Another reason to read history is to better understand the people of the past, and all the different cultures and nations that have existed, so that you can begin to determine which human behaviors are human nature and which are cultural. When I read Herodotus, and he describes many dozens of distinct peoples living in just one area of the Mediterranean in just one small slice of time, each with their own wildly different customs and societies, the diversity of human experience across time seems overwhelming. History is boundless, and is only limited by the extent to which we've written things down, and found archeological evidence. There will always be more of it to explore.

Myth is just as important as history. Read myth alongside history, with equal respect, because it has just as much a role in shaping humanity. Myth is the sister of history.
